entries.title: Trevon Williams brings the energy as Ag. Science beats Goode to win the Red Southwest
entries.summary: <p>The opening kickoff of a high school football game is rarely notable, but <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/10/08/high-school-football-scores-week-8" >Thursday</a> at Goode it was a preview of what was to come in a conference championship-deciding game between Ag. Science and the host Knights.</p><p>Ag. Science senior Trevon Williams burst past every player on the field and flattened Goode’s kick returner, setting the tone for the Cyclones’ 31-24 win.</p><p>“He’s been like that since he was a freshman,” Ag. Science coach Pat Ade said. “He started as a freshman and was quiet the first two years. He’s a lot more vocal now. He means so much to this team. He is definitely one of our big-time leaders.”</p><p>Williams caught a 14-yard touchdown pass in the first quarter and had five catches for 98 yards, while also playing a key defensive role in slowing down Goode’s high-powered rushing attack.</p><p>“Every game I try to bring the most energy I can and lift my team up,” Williams said.</p><p>Goode (5-2, 4-1) turned the ball over to Ag. Science on fumbles on its first three possessions and trailed 19-0 in the first quarter.</p><p>But the Knights charged back. Aedan Cleveland’s 36-yard TD run midway through the third quarter cut Ag. Science’s lead to 19-18. Then Goode cut the deficit to one point again with 9:31 left when Gabriel Chambers-Crosby got loose for a 50-yard touchdown run.</p><p>“They locked in and got focused,” Knights coach Terrence McClarn said. “A lot of teams would have crumbled, but our guys pulled it together. We have to work on our mistakes and eliminate those fumbles.”</p><p>Ag. Science (7-1, 4-0) sealed the win with an 11-yard touchdown run by James Gregory with 6:55 left, followed by a couple of big defensive stops.</p><p>“Trying to keep up with [Goode’s] run game is something we have been worried about all season,” Ade said. “They just do a heck of a job. We changed it up after halftime, and kind of slowed it down. They went back to the middle stuff and changed it up again.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b00000" name="image-b00000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dd43766/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+39/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F42%2Ff8%2F55cc581b41c8aa1c77dc66e3b9e5%2Fob-cst-091026-7009.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9ded617/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+39/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F42%2Ff8%2F55cc581b41c8aa1c77dc66e3b9e5%2Fob-cst-091026-7009.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c715f11/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+39/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F42%2Ff8%2F55cc581b41c8aa1c77dc66e3b9e5%2Fob-cst-091026-7009.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ag. Science coach Patrick Ade celebrates as the Cyclones wrap up the conference championship with a 31-24 victory over Goode." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c715f11/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+39/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F42%2Ff8%2F55cc581b41c8aa1c77dc66e3b9e5%2Fob-cst-091026-7009.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e541671/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+39/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F42%2Ff8%2F55cc581b41c8aa1c77dc66e3b9e5%2Fob-cst-091026-7009.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c715f11/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2000x1122+0+39/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F42%2Ff8%2F55cc581b41c8aa1c77dc66e3b9e5%2Fob-cst-091026-7009.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ag. Science coach Patrick Ade celebrates as the Cyclones wrap up the conference championship with a 31-24 victory over Goode.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Allen Cunningham/For the Sun Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Chambers-Crosby had five carries for 107 yards. Cleveland finished with 11 carries for 133 yards and 2 TDs. Alexander Holt added seven carries for 40 yards.</p><p>“Our guys kept answering the bell,” Ade said. “It looked like a funeral [after Goode’s comeback], but some big plays got us back up. That’s what we needed.”</p><p>Ag. Science quarterback Braeden Gillie went 11-for-19 for 176 yards and three touchdowns. He connected with senior Taylor Johnson for a 41-yard and a 26-yard touchdown.</p><p>“All the guys have been working really hard,” Johnson said. “We’ve been working outside of practice by ourselves. That really helped our chemistry and got us to the point we are at now.”</p><p>Both teams played in the state playoffs last year and have qualified again this season. The Public League football schedule for next week is still to be determined. Several White Division teams will play against Red Division teams to try and qualify for the state playoffs.</p><p>“This was a really important game,” Johnson said. “We are in the Red for the first time in school history and managed to win conference the first year. I’m glad we got to bring home the win for the guys and my coach.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Big Public League game this afternoon and Ag. Science strikes first. <br><br>Braeden Gillie to Taylor Johnson for a 41-yard TD.<br><br>Cyclones lead Goode 7-0. <a href="https://t.co/OGfTBYcoJV">pic.twitter.com/OGfTBYcoJV</a></p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2108302499283083292?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 8, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Hundreds of Lincoln Park High School students walk out in solidarity with Jane Doe in Cornell rape case
entries.summary: <p>Several hundreds of students walked out of Lincoln Park High School on Thursday afternoon in solidarity with Jane Doe, the former Cornell University student who alleged she was raped by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity at the Ivy League school in 2024.</p><p>The case has drawn widespread attention after <a class="Link" href="https://www.cornellsun.com/article/2026/09/tccsuykuvb4z" target="_blank" >the woman filed a lawsuit against Cornell</a> and the seven men accused of raping her. In the lawsuit, she alleges Cornell took insufficient action in response to her initial allegations. The woman filed as "Jane Doe," common in lawsuits where the accuser doesn't want their name made public.</p><p>The crowd stretched several blocks as students marched from Oz Park through the Lincoln Park neighborhood. Students chanted “No means no” throughout the walk and held signs declaring “Women’s rights are human rights,” “Intoxication is not an invitation,” and “If it’s not yes, it’s no.”</p><p>Key organizers of the walkout, Isabella Scaffai and Elianna St.Martin, were among the seniors leading the march, while several students gave short speeches throughout the walk. (Scaffai is the daughter of a staff member at WBEZ.)</p><p>St.Martin, 17, said the walkout was organized Thursday in support of student walkouts taking place nationally the same day.</p><p>“We just want to be a part of that and show our support for all the Jane Does around the world because more people need to speak out about these issues because just staying silent isn’t going to bring the change that we want to happen,” St.Martin said.</p><p>Several other students also spoke about sexual violence and standing in solidarity with friends and loved ones who had experienced sexual assault.</p><p>Senior Laila Sharda, 17, said the case has made her more critical of Ivy League universities and prompted her to rethink where she wants to attend college.</p><p>“It is such an abomination that these Ivy League schools think that they can pay their way out of real issues,” Sharda said. “I want to make sure that I'm in a college that respects me and respects my boundaries."</p><p>Sharda had also been keen on joining Greek life at university, but said the case has made her increasingly skeptical of fraternities and sororities.</p><p>Senior Luis Torres, 17, said he believes several of the “Cornell 7” weren't punished enough by the university.</p><p>“It’s completely unjustified how people at Cornell University only had the audacity to just expel two of their kids and make the others write essays,” Torres said. “I find that completely unbelievable.”</p><p>Near the end of the march, several students began chanting, “My body,” with the crowd responding, “My choice.”</p><p>“We are all Jane Does until no one is Jane Doe,” Scaffai told the crowd.</p>
entries.author: Misha Manjuran Oberoi

entries.title: Judge threatens to order Midway Blitz agents to hand over personal phones — after Bovino refused
entries.summary: <p>A federal judge in Chicago warned the Trump administration Thursday that any Homeland Security employee<b> </b>who worked Operation Midway Blitz might be ordered to turn over their personal phones for review — if litigation over the deportation campaign moves forward.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Sara<b> </b>Ellis<b> </b>did not explicitly order the phones be turned over. She <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/02/federal-judge-told-things-are-no-longer-quiet-as-midway-blitz-lawsuit-faces-critical-november-ruling" target="_blank" >has yet to rule</a> on whether she will even let the lawsuit move forward. But she told a Justice Department attorney she expects the government to make her intentions known, so data is not lost.</p><p>“It’s clear to me that agents were using their personal phones for work communication,” Ellis said. “And what I won’t allow to happen … is for people to hide behind saying that ‘these are our personal phones,’ when they are being used as work phones.”</p><p>Such an order would likely meet a significant challenge from the Trump administration. A government lawyer warned her that a similar order already met resistance in California, where<b> </b>the feds unleashed Operation At Large<b> </b>before turning their attention to Chicago.</p><p>Ellis has gone head-to-head with Midway Blitz officials before, though, even ordering<b> </b>then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/24/federal-judge-orders-border-patrol-commander-greg-bovino-into-her-courtroom" target="_blank" >into her courtroom</a><b> </b>last October. She referenced her experience with Bovino on Thursday, noting that “I have a hard time crediting what Mr. Bovino says.”</p><p>“It’s documented that he has a hard time telling the truth,”<b> </b>Ellis said. “Even when he’s under oath.”</p><p>Ellis presides over the lawsuit brought by Illinois and Chicago against Homeland Security. It alleges Midway Blitz was designed to coerce the state and city into assisting the federal government with its aggressive deportation efforts.</p><p>Ellis is set to rule Nov. 17 on Homeland Security’s bid to have the lawsuit tossed out.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/02/federal-judge-told-things-are-no-longer-quiet-as-midway-blitz-lawsuit-faces-critical-november-ruling" >Federal judge told ‘things are no longer quiet’ as Midway Blitz lawsuit faces critical November ruling</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Last fall, Ellis handled separate litigation over the feds’ use of force during Midway Blitz. That’s how she wound up ordering Bovino into her courtroom. She tried to force him to appear regularly in her courtroom, over the course of a week, to discuss his agents’ actions.</p><p>The federal appeals court in Chicago<b> </b>intervened, insisting the move <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/31/bovinos-daily-meetings-with-judge-would-infringe-on-separation-of-powers-appeals-court-says" target="_blank" >violated the separation of powers</a> between the courts and the executive branch. The appeals court also vacated<b> </b>a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >preliminary injunction</a> Ellis<b> </b>later<b> </b>handed down, which governed the agents’ use of force.</p><p>That litigation largely came to an end<b> </b>in January.</p><p>But Thursday, Ellis met with lawyers to discuss evidence in the new lawsuit brought by Illinois and Chicago. Among other things, Justice Department attorneys<b> </b>Lee Reeves and<b> </b>Jonathan<b> </b>Robbins explained efforts to preserve data from Bovino’s work and personal phones following Bovino’s retirement last spring.</p><p>Bovino<b> </b>reported<b> </b>a work phone as lost<b> </b>in January while traveling<b> </b>between<b> </b>Minnesota<b> </b>and South Dakota, records show. U.S. Customs and Border Protection<b> </b>failed to recover it despite<b> </b>tracking down<b> </b>its last known location and<b> </b>dispatching<b> </b>officers<b> </b>there, according to the feds.</p><p>Still, data from the lost work phone was stored online and is now preserved, Reeves assured Ellis.</p><p>However, Bovino<b> </b>also<b> </b>refused<b> </b>to surrender his<b> </b>personal phone for a government review ordered<b> </b>by<b> </b>a federal judge<b> </b>in California, records show. Bovino<b> </b>apparently told officials<b> </b>it<b> </b>contained<b> </b>no<b> </b>work-related data.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" >Judge blasts Trump’s Chicago border ‘Blitz,’ extends curbs on use of force that ‘shocks the conscience’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>But that’s left lawyers with few options, Illinois<b> </b>attorney<b> </b>Vikas<b> </b>Didwania told Ellis on Thursday.</p><p>“The only other way for us to access that information is to get it from the folks [Bovino] was communicating with,” Didwania said. “The people on the other side.”</p><p>Eventually, Ellis gave the Justice Department lawyers a “preview”<b> </b>of her thinking, which she said depends on “what survives”<b> </b>the pending motion to dismiss the case.</p><p>“Anyone currently employed by DHS, CBP and [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement] who was working, assigned to Operation Midway Blitz, that they will need to turn over their personal phones to be imaged,” Ellis said, “so that you can then go through and see which of them were discussing the operation with Mr. Bovino and each other.”</p><p>When warned about the litigation that might ensue, Ellis said she’d be “open to hearing about less intrusive ways to get this information.”</p><p>But, she said, she won’t let people hide behind their use of personal phones for work, “especially when there are directives, agency directives, that say they’re not to use their personal phones for work.”</p><p>“So we’ll find the least intrusive way to get this information,” Ellis said. “But we’re going to get this information.”</p>
entries.author: Jon Seidel
